title: True or False?
description: Meet Booleans, values that are either True or False, and how to compare things.

content.text: A switch is on or off, never in between. A **Boolean** is a data type with only two values: `True` or `False`. It is how Python answers a yes or no question.

items: You met booleans in the last module.
Now you will start **making** them yourself.
Capital first letter, and no quotes.
content.title: The big idea

content.value:
game_over = False
logged_in = True
print(game_over)
print(logged_in)

items.title: Breaks
items.text: Lowercase `true` is an error. `"True"` in quotes is a string, not a boolean.

content.question: Which line stores a boolean?
content.explain: `False` with a capital F and no quotes is a boolean. Lowercase `false` is an error, and quotes make it a string.

items: A **comparison operator** asks a question about two values.
The answer is always a boolean: `True` or `False`.
content.title: Asking Python a question

content.value: Try the lab below: change the numbers, change the operator, and watch the answer flip between True and False.

items.sub: Also True when both sides match: `7 >= 7` is `True`
Also True when both sides match: `4 <= 4` is `True`
Are both sides exactly the same? `2 == 4` is `False`

parts.label: operator
parts.note: The question: is the left side greater than or equal to the right side?

parts.label: right
parts.note: The second value. Here both sides match, so `>=` says `True`.

content.value:
print(5 > 3)
print(2 == 4)
print(10 != 9)
print(7 >= 7)    # True, because they are equal

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `<` asks if 5 is smaller than 5. They are equal, so the answer is `False`. Only `<=` would also count the equal case.

items.title: =  stores
items.text: One `=` puts a value in a variable.

items.title: ==  asks
items.text: Two `==` ask whether two values match. The answer is `True` or `False`.

content.title: One equals sign or two?
content.caption: Mixing up `=` and `==` is the most common beginner mistake in this module. Read `==` as "is equal to?".

content.question: Which line asks whether `lives` is 3?
content.explain: Two equals signs ask the question. One equals sign would store 3 in `lives` instead.

items: Like any value, you can store it in a variable.
Work out the answer once, then use it later.

parts.label: name
parts.note: The variable that will hold the answer.

parts.label: store
parts.note: One `=`: store whatever the right side works out to.

parts.label: question
parts.note: Python works this out first. It becomes `True` or `False`.

content.code:
score = 12
passed = score >= 10
print(passed)
score = 4
print(score >= 10)

steps.note: Python works out the right side first: is `12 >= 10`? Yes, so `True` goes into `passed`.
Change `score` to `4`. The `passed` box keeps its old answer: it was worked out back on line 2.
A fresh comparison: is `4 >= 10`? No, so this prints `False`.

content.title: Watch the answer get saved
content.outro: A saved answer does not update by itself. Compare again when the values change.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `9 >= 7` is `True`, and that answer is stored in `can_ride`, so printing it shows `True`.

practice.question: Make a variable called 'my_guess' that checks whether 8 is equal to 8. Then print it.
Store a score of 7 in a variable, then make a boolean called 'passed' that checks whether the score is 10 or more. Print it.

quiz.question: Which symbol checks if two values are equal?
quiz.explain: Use a double equals sign == to compare two values. A single = stores a value in a variable, and != means 'not equal'.

quiz.question: What does 5 != 5 give you?
quiz.explain: != means 'not equal'. Since 5 is equal to 5, the answer is False.

quiz.question: What does 7 >= 7 give you?
quiz.explain: >= means 'greater than or equal to'. The two sides are equal, so it is True.
